newsitem.title: GERMANY: Key statements by G7 leaders on currencies.
newsitem.headline: Key statements by G7 leaders on currencies.

text.p: Following are key statements on currency matters by officials from the Group of Seven industrialised nations who met in Berlin on Saturday:

The official statement issued by the seven nations -- the U.S., Germany, Japan, France, Italy, Canada and Britain -- said "We discussed the developments on currency and financial markets. We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected.
"We reaffirmed our views that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable.
"We agreed to monitor developments on the currency markets and to coooperate as appropriate."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said a strong dollar is in the United States' interest and suggested developments in the Japanese economy bear watching.
"A strong dollar is (in) the U.S. interest. We have had a strong dollar for some time now," Rubin told a news conference.
Rubin declined to say how exchange rate developments would be monitored and also refused to comment on the possibility of exchange rate intervention.

A senior U.S. Treasury official who declined to be named said the G7 has not sought a dollar appreciation for some time. "For some time now, the asymmetric position of April 1995 (pointing toward appreciation of the dollar) has not been the policy," the U.S. official said.

The U.S. official said the G7 agreement recognizes that the recent decline in the currencies of a number of the group's members are a "matter of concern." Those members include Japan and some European countries.
British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the G7 did not reach any agreement on concerted foreign exchange intervention.
"We reached no agreement of that kind today. We didn't think it was necessary," Clarke said.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the subject of intervention was not even discussed. "We will of course closely...cooperate, if necessary. What means are needed, we will discuss then," Tietmeyer told Reuters Financial Television.
Tietmeyer also said he did not expect any exaggerated movements in foreign exchange markets and that G7 central banks would not orient their policies to currency rates.

Asked whether the current dollar level was good for German economic growth, Tietmeyer replied "it is not a question of a precise level. We have never commented specifically on that...but it is more or less in line."
Tietmeyer and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the dollar's correction from record lows should be completed now.
Tietmeyer said "the dollar correction process ought to end about now." He added "the mark remains a stable and therefore, strong currency."

Waigel said the dollar's moves signalled an orderly recovery. "The orderly reversal sought by the G7 has taken place," Waigel said. He also stressed that dollar gains were not due to the failings of Germany or Europe.

Waigel said Germany was currently satisfied with the dollar's levels. "We are satisfied with the dollar. Six months ago, we noted an incorrect development with the dollar exchange rate. We wanted a stronger dollar, and that is what we have."
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis also said he was satisfied with current foreign exchange rate levels.
"I think the recent appreciation in the dollar was logical and necessary," Arthuis told reporters. "I would like the new configuration of exchange rates to be stable and lasting."
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said he thought the recent fall of the yen had been "rather rapid."
"I think the yen's fall from the beginning of this year has been rather rapid, and the pace of the import price increase has also been accelerating," he told reporters after the meeting.
A senior Ministry of Finance official said the yen's downward correction was complete.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Ministry of Finance's international finance bureau, said Japan would cooperate in currency market intervention if the yen depreciated further but said the G7 had no specific dollar targets.
Antonio Fazio, Italy's central bank governor, said European currency fluctuations at current levels were acceptable.
-- Terence Gallagher, Berlin Newsroom, 49-30-2039810
